claims.text: Static and dynamic lattice distortions in HfNbTaTiZr can be represented by an effective-temperature scaling law.
Variations in atomic radii and interatomic separations produce intrinsic local lattice distortion in solid-solution alloys.
Static interatomic-length disorder and dynamic temperature fluctuations have similar effects that can be unified through effective temperature.
The effective-temperature scaling law can be converted into an effective Debye temperature for HfNbTaTiZr.
Local lattice distortion and interatomic-separation disorder modulate phonon scattering and thermal transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
Mapping lattice disorder to effective temperature recalibrates the phonon spectrum governing lattice thermal conductivity.
The proposed model can predict the lattice thermal conductivity separately from the electronic contribution.
The proposed separation reduces conflation of lattice and electronic transport relative to earlier analytical approaches.
Earlier Debye-based or DFT-elasticity approaches conflate lattice and electronic contributions and are less accurate for HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed model will improve lattice-conductivity prediction accuracy by approximately 20–30% relative to earlier approaches.
The claimed 20–30% improvement applies over 300–1200 K.
Lattice conduction dominates at 300–1200 K in defect-free HfNbTaTiZr.
Below 200 K, lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are comparable.
Separating lattice and electronic transport is less certain below 200 K because the two contributions are comparable.
The model is limited to compositionally single-phase HfNbTaTiZr with low oxygen and defect concentrations.
The model may not apply to samples with substantial microstructural inhomogeneity or impurity content.
Magnetic-field modulation combined with thermal and electrical measurements can isolate or gauge the electronic thermal-conductivity contribution.
Deviation of predicted lattice thermal conductivity from measurements by more than ±30% across the target range would falsify the hypothesis.
